add_nodes.title: 300+ fully reusable heavy launches a year
add_nodes.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers fly 300 or more orbital missions in one calendar year, three times the 100-flight milestone.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Starship flew 5 times in 2025 and 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7. Approved site caps total about 145 Starship launches a year: Starbase 25 (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (Jan 2026) and SLC-37 76 (Dec 2025). Mach33's reference case has about 90 Starship flights in 2028 and about 516,000 t to orbit in 2040, 456,000 t of it SpaceX's own (Launch Keystone, Sep 2026), which implies thousands of flights a year by 2040.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor set by pads, propellant plants, environmental approvals and flights per stack. 300 flights a year is about one a day, so it needs roughly twice today's approved site caps plus new pads or offshore sites (2-4 years each; large transformers take 128-160 weeks). Demand comes from Starlink V3 and later, orbital compute (capability-compute-launch-demand) and lunar tanker campaigns. Chain (S2): 100+ flights 2030 -> new pads and raised caps 2031-32 -> 300+ flights 2033. S3 2032: cadence runs a year ahead and compute demand is stronger. S1 2034: the plateau weakens compute demand. AI moves cadence by months through anomaly closure and range scheduling. S4 gets no year credit: pads for this step are built 2030-32, while general construction robots arrive 2031-35, and approvals and airspace do not compress. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Bands (judgment): High by 2035 in S2-S4, because the S2 chain has two years of slack and the approval path already runs through named FAA environmental reviews (LC-39A, SLC-37, the New Glenn cap draft) under EO 14335; S1 Medium.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Starship has never met a yearly flight plan, and each failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months. Airspace closures, local opposition and litigation can cap cadence below what vehicles and pads allow.
add_nodes.signpost: 150 or more Starship flights in 2031 keeps S2 on track; a fourth Starship launch site approved; per-site caps raised above 100 a year.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 adds no year because approvals, airspace and pads built before construction robots set the pace.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-trunk (2026-10-07): new node extending the launch-clock side chain past physclock-heavy-cadence-100.

add_nodes.title: Starship internal cost under $100 per kg
add_nodes.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $100/kg, a third of the $300/kg milestone. Development, pads and factories are excluded.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026) cost about $4,915/kg with both stages expended (Mach33). Mach33's base case: $656/kg in 2027, about $300/kg in 2028, 8.9 flights per stack in 2029 and 18 in 2030, $13/kg in 2035 and $10/kg in 2040 (Launch Keystone v1.3, Sep 23, 2026).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor set by flights per stack, payload per flight and production learning (Mach33 splits the early decline 56% reuse, 32% payload, 12% learning). A $100M stack flying 18 times with $4M of operations and 112 t of payload costs about $85/kg (estimate), so the threshold needs ships flying about 10 times or more as well as boosters flying 20-30 times. The model dates $300/kg a year after Mach33 (2029 against 2028); the same lag puts $100/kg at about 2032 in every scenario, since AI moves the launch clock by months. Ship reuse at that count depends on the heat shield (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield, Medium by 2031), which keeps the node out of 2031. S4 gets no credit: reuse and payload set cost, and vehicles are already ahead of flights. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). High by 2035 in every scenario (judgment): Mach33's 2035 base sits about 8x below the threshold, so only a failure of ship reuse keeps cost above it.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: If tiles are a dead end for ship reuse, ships stay near single use and cost stays near $300/kg (a $40M ship over 150 t, plus booster and operations; estimate). Internal cost also does not reach customers: Mach33's median 2035 customer revenue is about $945/kg.
add_nodes.signpost: Disclosed ship flights per stack above 10; payload per flight near 150 t; SpaceX or Mach33 cost disclosures below $150/kg.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. The launch clock runs without AI math, so all four scenarios share the year, and S4 gets no credit.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-trunk (2026-10-07): new node extending the launch-clock side chain past physclock-cheap-mass-internal.

add_nodes.title: Leading firms halve development cycles
add_nodes.description: A leading commercial firm completes a new spacecraft or launch-vehicle program, started after AI adoption, at least 50% faster than its own comparable pre-2027 program, with a published schedule analysis. Typical programs are covered by capability-program-cycle-compression.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Fast commercial programs today: Starlink fields a new generation every 18-36 months, and Starship SN8-SN15 flew in 147 days with human crews. Only a few thousand humanoids do paid work, most need teleoperation (IFR, Sep 30, 2026), and none do flight-hardware assembly.
add_nodes.why: Amdahl with physics held fixed (s4-embodied): 2035 ceilings are about 42-52% in S2 (judgment from the model's program shares), 56% in S3, 58-62% in S4 for typical and leading programs, and 66-67% at robot-first firms. Realized gains run below ceilings: 40-48% in S3, 42-54% in S4 typical and leading, 50-58% at robot-first firms. Halving therefore needs a fast commercial program at the top of S3's range, or robots on most labor steps. Chain (S4): robots in paid flight-hardware work at leading firms 2030-31 -> process requalification, 6-24 months -> program started 2031 -> smallsat or derivative program finished in half its old time 2032-33 -> published analysis 2033. S3: programs started 2030-31 under near-free cognition finish 2033-34, so 2034. S1 and S2 stay after 2035 because their ceilings sit near or below 50%. S4 credit passes all four tests: integration, test and fabrication labor bind at the firm; robots are useful there from 2030-31; no hard prerequisite lands later; and general-purpose robots go beyond the specialized test stands already in S3. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) holds for S1 and S2. S3 is Low and S4 Medium (judgment), because 50% sits inside the robot-first realized range and at the top of S3's. Bands are judgments.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: At a robot-first firm in 2035, physics time constants, reliability statistics and institutions still make up about 44% of the remaining critical path, so one anomaly or a requalification dip erases the margin. Firms may spend the gain on scope, and attribution to AI and robots will be disputed.
add_nodes.signpost: A firm reports a new program at half the duration of its predecessor; humanoids in paid aerospace integration and test; the first robotic-process requalification for flight hardware.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. This is where S4 differs most in the trunk: about a year earlier than S3 and one band higher, carried by robot-first integration and test.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-trunk (2026-10-07): new node extending the spine past capability-program-cycle-compression; the main S4 outcome in the trunk.

add_nodes.title: A launcher or large spacecraft engineered mostly by AI flies
add_nodes.description: A launch-vehicle stage, a crew or cargo vehicle, or a spacecraft over 1 t dry mass whose design analyses, trade studies and flight-software verification artifacts were mostly AI-generated (with human review) flies and operates. The smallsat case is capability-ai-native-spacecraft.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. SpaceX owns a frontier lab (SpaceXAI), builds about 70 Starlink satellites a week (S-1/A) and flies Starlink V3 at about 2 t. AI-generated engine and structural geometry and agentic chip design exist piecemeal.
add_nodes.why: Second-generation step: the smallsat process outcome applied to a system with multiphysics margins, more interfaces and longer integration. Chain (S2): AI-native smallsat 2029 and design optimization 2028 -> a bus over 1 t or a stage designed mostly by AI 2029-30 -> build, integration and qualification in 18-30 months -> flies 2032. S3 2031: near-free cognition from 2029 and satellite generations compressed to 9-25 months. S1 2034: its smallsat lands in 2031. The likely first mover is a vertically integrated firm with its own models (SpaceX/SpaceXAI) on a satellite generation, where no certifier is involved. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) is raised because the physical step is routine for such firms; S2 Medium and S3 High by 2035 (judgment), S1 Low. As with the smallsat node, a majority AI share is hard to verify. S4 equals S3: design and disclosure bind, and integration robots add months at most. Bands are judgments.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Large systems carry more legacy process and liability, and firms may not publish what share AI produced. A launch stage is bound by hot fire and flight tests whoever designs it.
add_nodes.signpost: A satellite operator or launch firm publishes AI-generated verification evidence for a new bus or stage before flight, then reports on-orbit success.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 equals S3 because design work and disclosure bind, and robots on the build add months at most.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-trunk (2026-10-07): new node extending capability-ai-native-spacecraft to large systems.

patch.thesis: If research-grade AI math reaches outside engineers in 2027 (base case), on-demand analysis is routine in space engineering by 2028. Tests, factories and launches run on physical time, so schedules shrink 20-30% by 2031 and 30-40% by 2035. Robots (S4) add little before 2032; robot-first firms reach 50-58% by 2035.
